summary: This document presents requirements and a framework for point-to-multipoint pseudowires over MPLS packet networks. The requirements cover architecture, signaling and maintenance, and are meant as guidelines for developing standard mechanisms.

eli5.summary: A pseudowire is like a pretend cable across a network. This RFC asks how to make one pretend cable that splits so one sender can reach many receivers at once.

questions: how does p2mp pw reduce bandwidth usage
what is leaf grafting and pruning
subtitle: Extending pseudowires to send one stream to many receivers efficiently.

tldr.problem: Service providers need to deliver Layer 2 traffic from one source to multiple receivers, but existing point-to-point pseudowires require duplicating traffic at the source, wasting bandwidth on shared network links.
tldr.mechanism: Point-to-multipoint pseudowires extend the standard pseudowire architecture to create a single virtual tree where content is replicated only once by the network, not at the source, and reaches all leaf provider edges simultaneously.
tldr.outcome: P2MP pseudowires enable efficient multicast Layer 2 services like Virtual Private LAN Service and Virtual Private Multicast Service with bandwidth optimization equivalent to native multicast.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Single-segment pseudowires; multi-segment left for future work

facts.label: Multiplexing
facts.value: Multiple P2MP PWs can share one P2MP LSP

today: RFC 7338 is an informational requirements document that guides the development of P2MP pseudowire standards. Implementations continue to evolve in MPLS environments to support efficient multicast Layer 2 services in carrier networks.

sections.title: Pseudowires and the Multicast Challenge
sections.content:
A pseudowire (PW) is a mechanism that emulates a traditional telecommunications service (like a leased line or Frame Relay) over a modern packet network. It encapsulates Layer 1 or Layer 2 traffic, carrying it across an IP or MPLS network in a way that the endpoints perceive it as a direct link, even though it travels through a larger network.

Historically, pseudowires have been point-to-point: one source connects to one destination. However, services like Virtual Private LAN Service and Virtual Private Multicast Service require one-to-many connectivity. The naive solution—using multiple point-to-point pseudowires and replicating traffic at the source—wastes bandwidth on shared links that must carry the same traffic multiple times. Point-to-multipoint pseudowires solve this by using the underlying network's multicast capabilities, sending just one copy of each packet along the tree, with replication happening naturally in the network core.
sections.eli5: Normally a pretend cable goes from one place to one place. For group meetings, you need a pretend cable that one place can talk into and many places can listen to without the starting place having to say everything multiple times.

sections.title: Reference Architecture
sections.content:
A P2MP PW has a Root Provider Edge (PE) attached to the traffic source via an Attachment Circuit, and one or more Leaf Provider Edges attached to receiver attachment circuits. The Root PE sends traffic into a point-to-multipoint PSN tunnel (typically a P2MP MPLS Label Switched Path) that carries the pseudowire packets to all Leaf PEs. Each Leaf PE replicates the traffic to its local receiver attachment circuits.

The architecture considers three replication points: ingress PE replication to local customer edges, core network replication via the P2MP tunnel, and egress PE replication to local customer edges. By using P2MP tunnels, duplicate copies of each packet exist only where needed—at branching points in the network tree—rather than at the source.

The P2MP PW is normally unidirectional (from Root to Leaf), though the architecture optionally supports return paths from Leaf PEs back to the Root PE for upstream traffic.
sections.eli5: One person talks into a special network cable at the root. The cable splits like a tree: once at a junction in the network, then again where the leaves are. Each person on a leaf hears the same words the root person said, once each.

sections.title: Setting Up and Managing the Tree
sections.content:
Each P2MP PW must have a unique identifier used in all signaling procedures. The Root PE and Leaf PEs must be configured with the same pseudowire type so they know they are compatible. Interface parameters related to attachment circuit capabilities must be verified during setup; if a Leaf PE's attachment circuit cannot support the traffic, the PE must reject the join.

After the tree is established, leaf grafting (adding new Leaf PEs) and leaf pruning (removing Leaf PEs) must be supported without disrupting traffic to remaining leaves. Failure detection is critical: if a Leaf PE goes down, the Root PE must be notified so it can prune that branch and update the remaining leaves. Solutions must support both out-of-band monitoring (separate OAM) and in-band monitoring (using virtual circuit connectivity verification), with status notifications that clearly identify which Leaf PE failed.
sections.eli5: Everyone needs to agree they are using the same kind of cable. You can add or remove listeners without breaking the broadcast. If someone stops listening, the broadcaster needs to know right away.

sections.title: Reliability and Protection
sections.content:
The architecture assumes the underlying P2MP MPLS tunnel supports standard recovery techniques. Solutions must avoid race conditions where the tunnel level and the PW level try to recover at the same time. Leaf PEs can be protected using a redundancy mechanism where a standby P2MP PW mirrors the active one; if the active tree fails or if leaves are lost, traffic switches to the standby tree.

The Root PE can also be protected: two P2MP PWs originate from different Root PEs, and a single attachment circuit at each Leaf PE selects between them, automatically switching if one Root fails. The architecture must provide mechanisms for the Root PE to select which recovery strategy applies and under what conditions to switch.
sections.eli5: If the broadcast breaks, there can be a backup tree ready to take over. If the broadcaster fails, listeners can automatically switch to hearing from a backup broadcaster.

sections.title: Scalability Considerations
sections.content:
The solution must scale efficiently: memory requirements, message sizes, and CPU processing must grow at worst linearly with the number of Leaf PEs. Multiple P2MP PWs can be multiplexed onto a single P2MP LSP, so adding more pseudowires does not proportionally increase the number of forwarding table entries in core routers.

The multiplexing decision may be user-configured or automatic, based on overlap between the PW's Leaf PE set and existing LSP egress routers. Operators may define a minimum congruency rate (the percentage of overlap) below which multiplexing is not allowed to prevent non-leaf routers from receiving unwanted traffic. Since non-leaf routers drop traffic unless they have forwarding entries, no special configuration is needed to protect them.
sections.eli5: Adding more listeners does not make the network work much harder. Many group broadcasts can share the same tree branches to save space.

sections.title: Security and Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
P2MP PW solutions must be backward compatible with existing point-to-point pseudowire standards, reusing existing capability advertisement and negotiation procedures. Solutions must not allow a P2MP PW to be set up to PEs that do not support P2MP functionality, and must report clear errors when incompatible endpoints are discovered.

Security requirements include protecting delivered traffic against eavesdropping, modification, and spoofed endpoints through mechanisms like encryption and authentication. The solution must defend against denial-of-service attacks, including safeguards to prevent attacks on one receiver from harming the entire tree. Both data plane and control plane security must be considered to prevent attackers from injecting false status notifications or modifying signaling messages.
sections.eli5: The system must not break old single-person cables. Everyone must verify they support the group feature. Bad people must not be able to break the broadcast or spy on it.
